title: The accessibility contract reaches a consumer only as prose the package does not carry
foundBy: consumer-facing test: two agents given an installed copy both reconstructed the accessibility contract by reading compiled JavaScript

evidence.verified:
`npm run ci` exits 0 with 84 test files where there were 83, the visual gate at 112 of 112 captures and 0 differing pixels, axe at 0 rules matching more nodes, and `size:subpaths` passing. The package grew from 119.0 kB to 120.4 kB.

Measured on the artifact rather than the source, which is the failure mode a dev-only guard invites. `dist/lib/formWiringWarning.js` ships at 1447 bytes with its `process.env.NODE_ENV` guard intact and is imported by `dist/lib/forwardRefToRoot.js`. The built file was then run: given a FormGroup-shaped node with a label and no `htmlFor`, and one with helper text nothing refers to, it emitted both warnings; given a correctly wired one it emitted none; and with `NODE_ENV=production` set it emitted nothing at all. That is the published file warning, not the source.

The tests were proved able to fail by mutation. Neutering the label predicate failed one test of six; neutering the describedby predicate failed two, which are the helper case and the error case. The file was restored and `git diff` read clean.

The tests drive the predicate with DOM a real FormGroup rendered rather than a fixture written to match it, and each takes a fresh module instance, so none of them depends on the order the others ran in. The check warns once per kind of mistake, which is right on a page of twenty broken fields and would otherwise let a later test assert on silence it had not earned.

No false positives in this repository: all 19 `FormGroup` usages across `preview/`, `patterns/` and `src/` pass `htmlFor`, except CheckboxGroup's own internal wrap, which is the composite case the warning deliberately allows and which has a test of its own.

details:
What a component guarantees to assistive technology is written in `components/<Name>.md`, and those documents do not ship. The type declarations that do ship carry almost none of it: 4 of about 38 declaration files mention `aria-` at all.

So a consumer holding the package has no machine-readable account of the contract. Two agents were each given an installed copy and asked how they would use the library. Both, independently and without being asked about accessibility, ended up reading `dist/components/*.js` to work out the wiring. Deriving a contract from compiled output is not reading documentation.

Both found the same two silent failures in `FormGroup`. It clones its child, and so supplies `id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid` and `required`, only when it has exactly one valid element child; a second child drops all four with no error. And its label carries `htmlFor` only when the consumer passes one, so omitting it leaves the label unassociated while the control still receives a generated id. Both are the kind of defect that ships and is found by an audit.

The recommendation is to split the contract by shape rather than to move it wholesale. Where a guarantee is bound to a prop, it belongs in that prop's TSDoc, which is already the practice: `FormGroup`'s `htmlFor` carries exactly that prose today, and both agents quoted it. The gap there is coverage rather than approach.

Where a guarantee has no prop to attach to, TSDoc cannot hold it. The single-child rule is a fact about children, and documenting it on an unrelated prop puts it where nobody looks. For those the kit already has a better instrument in `src/lib/stylesheetWarning.ts` and its neighbour `clippedContentWarning`: a warning in the consumer's development build, at the moment the mistake is made.

notes.text: The obstacle that would otherwise sink a runtime warning is already solved here. `src/lib/stylesheetWarning.ts` guards on `process.env.NODE_ENV` rather than on `import.meta.env.DEV`, and says why: the latter is replaced when this package is built, which would leave the check dead in every published copy and warn nobody. A new warning copies that guard, and whoever writes one confirms it survives into `dist/` rather than trusting that it does.

One judgement is left open and belongs to the owner. Putting an operative sentence in TSDoc while the full contract stays in the component document duplicates a fact, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` holds that every fact lives in exactly one place. The argument for accepting it is that the TSDoc carries a warning at the point of use rather than a second description of the behaviour. The argument against is that this repository is strict about that rule for good reasons, and a duplicated sentence drifts. Settle this before writing the first one.

Decided by the owner: the duplication is accepted, for prop-bound guarantees only. A short operative sentence may sit in a prop's TSDoc while the full contract stays in the component document, because the TSDoc is a warning at the point of use rather than a second description of the behaviour.

That is a deliberate exception to the rule in `CONTRIBUTING.md` that a fact lives in one place, and it is bounded: it does not license copying the contract wholesale. A guarantee with no prop to attach to, such as the rule that `FormGroup` wires nothing unless it has exactly one element child, still belongs in a development warning rather than in prose nobody reads.

Measured before writing anything, because the shape of the work depended on it. Twenty-four of 38 components carry an accessibility section, holding 84 bullets between them. Of those, five are operative and bound to a declared prop: CheckboxGroup `label`, FormGroup `htmlFor`, Input `error`, StatusBadge `announce` and Tooltip `describedBy`. FormGroup and Tooltip already carried theirs in TSDoc, so the coverage gap the record describes was three props, and those three now carry a sentence each.

The rest divide in two. Some are facts a consumer can break without being told, such as FormGroup wiring nothing unless it has one element child, and those are what the development warning is for. Most are facts a consumer cannot break at all, such as Modal rendering `role="dialog"`, and neither instrument helps with those: they are reference material, and the record does not ask for them to move.

The warning reads the DOM rather than the props, which is what turned up CUI-093. Checking the outcome asks whether anything refers to the helper's id, and that question makes visible where the reference landed. In CheckboxGroup it lands on a roleless `<div>`, so the helper is wired and still announced to nobody.

That is deliberately not what this warning tests. `FormGroup` cannot know what its child renders, so it cannot tell a control from a wrapper, and a predicate that guessed would warn on correct code. It is filed separately and belongs in `CheckboxGroup`.

The owner's exception is recorded in `CONTRIBUTING.md` beside the rule it bends, rather than only in this record, because a rule with an unwritten exception is one the next reader will enforce wrongly.
